doc.title: Iola Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, CT, July 17, 2011

title: Columbia royalties and starting their own publishing
summary: Early royalties from Jazz Goes to College, George Avakian's surprise, and learning they could form their own publishing company.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Wow. I’ll have to work on that for the Unitarian church that I play at. I’ll have to see if I can get that going. Back to paying dues. I don’t know if you would remember such an incident but would you remember the first time a check came to your house for one of Dave’s compositions? Like an ASCAP royalty or BMI or something like that?

No I don’t remember the first. Let me see. I remember a couple of things. I remember when Dave signed with Columbia he received an advance and of course there was royalties against the advance and I can remember being quite excited and surprised to see how fast he was able to reach that point to actually be receiving royalties, because he’d paid off the advance and was receiving royalties. Because “Jazz Goes to College” sold very well. And I remember George Avakian was surprised and we were all surprised that it sold as well as it did. That I remember.
And he would get slightly more money if he had his own compositions on the records too, wouldn’t he?
Well writer’s royalty? If he had his own tunes on the records as opposed to standards, did he get a little bit more?

Well that has a little history too. First he recorded all standards, and then at Columbia there were a few originals and they said, “Okay we’ll put them in our publishing company.” And we weren’t smart enough to know that you didn’t have to do that. And it wasn’t until we had some business management that said, “You know you can have your
own publishing company.” We thought aha, this is a revelation. So that made a very big difference.
I’m glad you found that out when you did.
I’m glad we found it out before “Time Out.”
